Choke no more: Can the Proteas Finally Break the Curse?

By: Nickolaus Bauer | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
It’s the final Test. The biggest stage. And South Africa are once again on the cusp of greatness — or another grand collapse. With the World Test Championship final against Australia set at the ic

Unique Selling Point:
Told through the eyes of a long-suffering Proteas fan, this piece is part comedy, part catharsis — a generational therapy session disguised as a cricket feature. It’s a story about hope, heartbreak, and the strange, stubborn love of South African fans who keep coming back for more.


Summary:
For decades, the Proteas have found heartbreak in the most imaginative ways possible, from farcical rain rules in 1992 to boundary drama in 2023. Now, with the World Test Championship final against Australia set at the iconic Lord’s Cricket Ground, can the national team finally exorcise the ghosts of cricketing trauma past?
Told through the eyes of a long-suffering Proteas fan, this piece is part comedy, part catharsis — a generational therapy session disguised as a cricket feature. It’s a story about hope, heartbreak, and the strange, stubborn love of South African fans who keep coming back for more.


Further information:
Key Themes:
The Curse of the Proteas:
Revisiting South Africa’s most painful cricketing moments:
1992: 22 needed off 1 ball vs. England
1996: Brian Lara’s masterclass knocks us out
1999: Allan Donald drops his bat, World Cup dream dies
2003: Shaun Pollock misreads Duckworth-Lewis
2007: Batting collapse against Australia
2011: Demolished by the Pakistanis
2015: Rain, heartbreak, and Elliott’s six
2023: David Miller's boundary catch — out or over?
The Psychology of Choking:
Can national trauma be inherited? Is performance pressure a self-fulfilling prophecy? What makes teams crumble — and what might finally help us break through?
Fans on the Edge:
For South Africans who’ve travelled the world to watch the Proteas, this isn’t just another match. It’s a spiritual reckoning.
Hope, Humor, and Holding On:
From bookies giving odds on a classic South African collapse, to fan parks full of cheering (and weeping) expats — this is a love story, set to leather and willow.

Visual Approach:
Bookends at Lord’s:
Opening shot: the hallowed Long Room at Lord’s on Day 1 — Nickolaus in full fan regalia.
Closing shot: same spot on Day 5 — outcome unknown, but the heart remains.
Fan Parks, Living Rooms & Labs:
Footage of Sipho Van Der Merwe waving a flag in the crowd and FaceTiming his family back home
Animated reenactments of cricket heartbreaks (think: comic-style renderings of Donald’s runout, Lara’s boundary blitz)
A quirky interview with Thomas Winalot, taking absurd bets on new ways South Africa might lose
Interview scenes with Prof. Winter, surrounded by data, graphs, and slow-mo collapses
Nostalgic cricket archive visuals: broken stumps, stunned faces, flying bails
Voice, Tone, and Music:
Hopeful yet haunted.
A mix of emotional scoring and cheeky cricketing commentary
Daniel Gallan providing the voice of weary, informed optimism
Ntini as the heartbeat of belief: “This is the one.”

Scene Breakdown:
Scene 1: Day One – The Wait Begins
Location: Lord’s Cricket Ground, London
Nickolaus Bauer (PTC):
“They say hope is a dangerous thing. For Proteas fans, it’s also hereditary. But here we are again — finals day, full of belief, with just a little PTSD.”
VO:
"Thirty years. Five formats. One long heartbreak. The Proteas have made a habit of turning opportunity into agony."

Scene 2: A Fan’s Tale
Location: Tube ride to Lord’s, then the stands
Sipho Van Der Merwe:
“I’ve mortgaged my sanity to this team. But I wouldn’t miss this for the world. This could be the day we finally heal.”

Scene 3: Trauma in HD
Location: Studio reenactments & archive clips
VO:
“1992. Rain falls, hopes drown. 1999. One bat drop, one heartbreak. 2023. A toe on the rope, a nation weeps.”
Pollock (reflecting):
“We were so close. But sometimes, the weight of history... you feel it.”

Scene 4: The Choke Explained
Location: Academic lab
Prof. Stacy Winter:
“Choking isn’t about skill. It’s about what happens when self-doubt hijacks performance. South Africa? They've built an identity around almost.”

Scene 5: The Bookmaker’s Bet
Location: London betting shop
Thomas Winalot:
“Odds of SA collapsing from a winning position? We’ve got a name for that: the Proteas Special.” (laughs)

Scene 6: The Final Hour
Location: Lord’s, Day 5
VO:
"Whether it ends in triumph or tears, this is the price of believing. Because to be a Proteas fan is to love without condition."

Scene 7: Ending – After the Final Ball
Location: Long Room at Lord’s, sunset
Nickolaus Bauer (PTC):
“We laughed. We cried. We hoped. And no matter the result, we’ll be back next time. Because this team? This pain? It’s family.”

Outcome Possibilities:
If Proteas Win:
"We exorcised the demon."
Emotional montages, fans crying, Ntini dancing in the stands, Daniel Gallan speechless.
If Proteas Lose:
"What did you expect?"
Sipho eating a wors roll in silence, a child with a broken vuvuzela, bookie paying out smug bets — and Nickolaus quietly hopeful for 2029

- Flights from Madrid to London
- Videographer for 2-3 days

Press Release:


What does it take to break a curse? It was the final Test. The biggest stage. South Africa hovered once again on the cusp of greatness — or another grand collapse. For decades, the Proteas have found heartbreak in the most imaginative ways possible. Now, in
the World Test Championship final against Australia, has the national team finally exorcised the ghosts of cricketing trauma past? It’s a story of hope and heartbreak, of loyalty against the odds… and of long-suffering, devoted fans rewarded at long last.
Carte Blanche celebrates with our national team.

Script:


(Archive Upsound) Pakistan today played the better cricket.



(Archive Upsound) South Africa would be shocked.



(Archive Upsound) South Africa were the firm favourites. But not anymore.



(Nickolaus Graphics On Screen) Redemption after years of suffering. For over three decades, the Proteas - our men's national cricket team - provided agony and despair for their fans, failing to win when it mattered.



(Archive Upsound) South Africa will be desperately disappointed with that.



(Nickolaus) Until now… Last weekend, a team long criticised as chokers – the dreaded C-word – finally performed at Lord’s cricket ground in London, England. But it wouldn’t be an easy ride.



(Archive Upsound) There they are. Champagne in the air. The celebrations. A successful Test Championship final.



(Nickolaus) The home of cricket, the World Test Championship final and South Africa versus Australia. Another opportunity to exorcise the choking curse as a Proteas fan. I'm going to leave nothing to chance. I'm even wearing my lucky socks!



(Nickolaus) Supporting the Proteas has become an exercise in generational trauma. From sheer bad luck, rain and the dreaded Duckworth-Lewis scoring system to batting capitulations and demolitions of our bowling. The Proteas have always found a way to snatch defeat from the jaws of victory.



(Voxie Female 1) Respect on both sides, but SA is going to bring the cup home, I’m afraid.



(Nickolaus) Lord’s, generally regarded as cricket’s spiritual home, would be the stage for yet another shot at glory.



(Archive Upsound) What an uptake.



(Nickolaus) Altogether, the Proteas have failed 13 times in global tournaments over 33 years. It’s a record cricket correspondent, Daniel Gallan says is impossible to ignore every time they play.



(Daniel Gallan) So many heartaches - 92 in the rain, Allan Donald dropped bat in 99, the poor maths in 2003, New Zealand chokes losing to the Netherlands, India last year in the T20 final. I guess we South African cricket fans who have suffered for so long feel like we're due one maybe.



(Nickolaus) How does this Proteas team stack up against the others that couldn’t get across the line?



(Daniel Gallan) I think that they're more than the sum of their parts. I think there's a sense of unity. I think there's a collective. And I think that, unlike previous iterations… I maybe have strong memories of past chokes. They are free from this narrative. At least, that's the line that they're trying to cultivate. And I do think there's a sincerity in that.



(Nickolaus) London is a long way from Cape Town, Durban and Johannesburg. But that didn’t stop these fans from making their way here.



(Voxie Male 1) We’re South Africans, we love sports. It's in our DNA.



(Voxie Female 2) They're an awesome team. And we've got to get behind our boys. And they're only going to win if we come and support them and cheer them on.



(Voxie Male 2) We win, we win. If we lose, we take it on the chin.



(Voxie Male 3) Yes, there’s been heartache. Yes, there’s been very, very tough times. But again, you wake up, dust yourself off and you go again.



(Voxie Male 4) Hopefully, you can split the choke out consistently over five days.



(Voxie Male 5) Temba Bavuma! Wonderful!



(Nickolaus) Could it be the Test World Championship - a tournament including the top nine teams in the game’s longest format - that would finally deliver victory? As a diehard Proteas fan myself, I hoped so.



(Nickolaus) The limitless optimism of Proteas fans didn’t do much to better the odds of them finally winning a trophy. William Kedjanyi is a bookie specialising in cricket betting.



(Nickolaus) I'm loath to use the C-word, but we haven't had the best record when it comes to knockout games. How do you think that's going to affect the odds?



(William Kedanyi) Some people have labelled the Proteas a bottling premium, even in betting circles, waiting for them to choke so it improves their position. But I think this time, people might just be overrating that factor a little bit. You have to treat each game as it is. There are factors that will push prices and bring them in.



(Nickolaus) So, if I'm a betting man, what are the odds for the Proteas against Australia?



(William Kedanyi) They are 25%, or 3 to 1. Now look, that will seem low. It will seem pessimistic. But it's not really against the Proteas. It's Australia. The guys going in there, they'll know exactly what they're doing. And it's not to say South Africa won't, but you look at it, it's a very menacing line-up.



(Nickolaus) In other words: don’t bet on the Proteas unless you’re comfortable losing your money. Something I’m certainly not.



(Nickolaus) While they might have been against us, I still felt confident our team would beat the odds. Finally turning the tide on a losing habit that began back at the 1992 World Cup in Australia. After cruising to victory in a match against England, the weather intervened, leaving us needing 22 runs off just one ball.



(David Richardson) Back in those days, you had a profession and played cricket.



(Nickolaus) You were a lawyer, weren’t you?



(David Richardson) Yes, I was.



(Nickolaus) Former Proteas wicket-keeper, David Richardson was at the crease at the time.



(David Richardson) It's something that I look back on and think, “Gee! That was an opportunity that was missed.”



(Nickolaus) Sometimes, it feels as though the Proteas are cursed.



(David Richardson) Well, maybe there is a curse. Who knows? But I still think that in their heart and soul, in the moment they are competing and it’s not a case of them just wilting under pressure. I think it's something that will either go your way or not. And you do need a bit of luck. On many occasions, even to the best to actually get over the line.



(Archive Upsound) South Africa against Australia. The sun is shining on Lord’s Cricket Ground. It is set up perfectly.



(Nickolaus) Armed with my accreditation, I joined hundreds of media from around the world covering the match.



(Archive Upsound) It is a batting day.



(Nickolaus) But compared to the stiffness of the media centre, the gees of the stands was hard to resist.



(Nickolaus) Duty calls.



(Nickolaus) Let’s go!



(Archive Upsound) Two top sides and a great format. Test match cricket is back!



(Nickolaus) Lord’s is hallowed ground for any cricket fan. And for the week of the Test Championship, it took on a distinctly South African flavour.



(Nickolaus Subtitles) A little taste of home, hey?



(Vendor Subtitles) The boerewors is sold out. They are…



(Nickolaus Subtitles) Sold out of Boerewors! Sold out of Boerewors!



(Nickolaus) Prior to the tournament, questions had been raised about whether we deserved to be in the final at all, not having played against all the sport’s top teams. We went into the game against a powerful Australian side as solid underdogs.



(Nickolaus) As Temba Bavuma led us into battle, I took my place in the stands.



(Nickolaus) After the Aussies were put in to bat, our bowling attack didn’t disappoint.



(Archive Upsound) And there it is. What a moment for Kagiso Rabada.



(Nickolaus) Restricting Australia to 212 in their first innings after an aggressive KG Rabada took 5 wickets.



(Archive Upsound) So, wickets continue to tumble after lunch. It’s 137 for 8.



(Nickolaus) Then, as had been the case so often before, optimism gave way to frustration as the Aussie bowlers had us all out for 138… 74 runs behind! The ghosts of past failures came back to haunt me.



(Archive Upsound) Bowled-out South Africa out for 138. Which gives them a very healthy lead of 74.



(Nickolaus) Our cricket team is the opposite of fairytale character Peter Pan, which doesn't exist unless you believe in it. The Proteas, on the other hand, fail to exist the moment you believe in them. Why?



(Nickolaus) Why had the Proteas managed to flop every single time it mattered since 1992?



(Nickolaus) Sports psychologist Kitrina Douglas had some interesting thoughts.



(Kitrina Douglas) I'm curious to see how all the other cricket teams’ story, their experiences, their losses… And I'd be interested to look at the games that you are winning and what's happening there and how that is storied by the media, by the press, by the fans. Is that given a negative slant?



(Nickolaus) Hang on, Professor. You’re saying that we, the fans, are the problem?



(Kitrina Douglas) Yes, I am actually. And I think psychology more recently has expanded to realise that it's not just about what happens inside here. It's about what happens in your immediate subculture, in the culture and society what cricket means for them. Because the dominant narrative is it's all about winning, it's all about being the best. And that's what we want. And anything short of that is failure. So, I think the first thing is to support the players, whatever, and not put your expectations on them.



(Crowd) Oh, Temba Bavuma! Oh, Temba Bavuma!



(Nickolaus) Doing my best to heed the advice, I headed back to the stands. What followed was a pulsating four days of test cricket, not all of it easy to watch.



(Archive Upsound) Frustration again. Just dabbed away up the hill.



(Nickolaus) Our bowlers again pulled off a minor miracle in restricting Australia to 207 in their second innings, leaving a small window to victory - 282 needed for an improbable win.



(Nickolaus) Then Bavuma, after a reasonable score in the first innings, look set for an early departure after apparently pulling a leg muscle.



(Nickolaus) And, after being out for a duck in his first knock, opening batsman Aiden Markram was hardly inspiring confidence in the traveling fans.



(Nickolaus) But our captain played through the pain, scoring runs and providing support to Makram who stuck it to his critics by scoring a brilliant century.



(Archive Upsound) And if South Africa go on to win this game, it will be his most important.



(Archive Upsound) Fantastic performance here by Aiden Markram.



(Archive Upsound) Verreyne does the honours. And South Africa make history.



(Nickolaus) After a nail-biting few sessions of cricket, the Proteas finally broke the curse, beating Australia by five wickets and becoming the 2025 World Test Championship winners.



(Archive Upsound) South Africa!



(Nickolaus) Choke no more!



(Daniel Gallan) I truly think this could be the greatest moment in South African cricket history.



(Nickolaus) For the man that led the way to breaking the curse with a disciplined 136 in the second innings, it was a moment to savour.



(Aiden Markram) Just to see the smiles on faces and the happy vibes from everyone supporting us has been really cool. A lot of this victory goes towards them. Those that have been there through thick and thin for us. And it's just as special for them as it is for us.



(Nickolaus) The Proteas can finally call themselves champions. Champions against Australia in the world test championship final at Lord’s.

Summary: For decades, the Proteas have found heartbreak in the most imaginative ways possible, from farcical rain rules in 1992 to boundary drama in 2023. Now, with the World Test Championship final against Australia set at the iconic Lord’s Cricket Ground, can the national team finally exorcise the ghosts of cricketing trauma past? Told through the eyes of a long-suffering Proteas fan, this piece is part comedy, part catharsis — a generational therapy session disguised as a cricket feature. It’s a story about hope, heartbreak, and the strange, stubborn love of South African fans who keep coming back for more. Further information: Key Themes: The Curse of the Proteas: Revisiting South Africa’s most painful cricketing moments: 1992: 22 needed off 1 ball vs. England 1996: Brian Lara’s masterclass knocks us out 1999: Allan Donald drops his bat, World Cup dream dies 2003: Shaun Pollock misreads Duckworth-Lewis 2007: Batting collapse against Australia 2011: Demolished by the Pakistanis 2015: Rain, heartbreak, and Elliott’s six 2023: David Miller's boundary catch — out or over? The Psychology of Choking: Can national trauma be inherited? Is performance pressure a self-fulfilling prophecy? What makes teams crumble — and what might finally help us break through? Fans on the Edge: For South Africans who’ve travelled the world to watch the Proteas, this isn’t just another match. It’s a spiritual reckoning. Hope, Humor, and Holding On: From bookies giving odds on a classic South African collapse, to fan parks full of cheering (and weeping) expats — this is a love story, set to leather and willow. Visual Approach: Bookends at Lord’s: Opening shot: the hallowed Long Room at Lord’s on Day 1 — Nickolaus in full fan regalia. Closing shot: same spot on Day 5 — outcome unknown, but the heart remains. A mix of emotional scoring and cheeky cricketing commentary Daniel Gallan providing the voice of weary, informed optimism Ntini as the heartbeat of belief: “This is the one.” Scene Breakdown: Scene 1: Day One – The Wait Begins Location: Lord’s Cricket Ground, London Nickolaus Bauer (PTC): “They say hope is a dangerous thing. For Proteas fans, it’s also hereditary. But here we are again — finals day, full of belief, with just a little PTSD.” VO: "Thirty years. Five formats. One long heartbreak. The Proteas have made a habit of turning opportunity into agony." Scene 2: A Fan’s Tale Location: Tube ride to Lord’s, then the stands Sipho Van Der Merwe: “I’ve mortgaged my sanity to this team. But I wouldn’t miss this for the world. This could be the day we finally heal.” Scene 3: Trauma in HD Location: Studio reenactments & archive clips VO: “1992. Rain falls, hopes drown. 1999. One bat drop, one heartbreak. 2023. A toe on the rope, a nation weeps.” Pollock (reflecting): “We were so close. But sometimes, the weight of history... you feel it.” Scene 4: The Choke Explained Location: Academic lab Prof. Stacy Winter: “Choking isn’t about skill. It’s about what happens when self-doubt hijacks performance. South Africa? They've built an identity around almost.” Scene 5: The Bookmaker’s Bet Location: London betting shop Thomas Winalot: “Odds of SA collapsing from a winning position? We’ve got a name for that: the Proteas Special.” (laughs) Scene 6: The Final Hour Location: Lord’s, Day 5 VO: "Whether it ends in triumph or tears, this is the price of believing. Carte Blanche HD nombuso@carteblanche.co.za 23 June 2025 TX Date: 0000-00-00 Press Release: What does it take to break a curse? It was the final Test. The biggest stage. South Africa hovered once again on the cusp of greatness — or another grand collapse. For decades, the Proteas have found heartbreak in the most imaginative ways possible. Now, in the World Test Championship final against Australia, has the national team finally exorcised the ghosts of cricketing trauma past? It’s a story of hope and heartbreak, of loyalty against the odds… and of long-suffering, devoted fans rewarded at long last. Carte Blanche celebrates with our national team. Script: (Archive Upsound) Pakistan today played the better cricket. (Archive Upsound) South Africa would be shocked. (Archive Upsound) South Africa were the firm favourites. But not anymore. (Nickolaus Graphics On Screen) Redemption after years of suffering. For over three decades, the Proteas - our men's national cricket team - provided agony and despair for their fans, failing to win when it mattered. (Archive Upsound) South Africa will be desperately disappointed with that. (Nickolaus) Until now… Last weekend, a team long criticised as chokers – the dreaded C-word – finally performed at Lord’s cricket ground in London, England. But it wouldn’t be an easy ride. (Archive Upsound) There they are. Champagne in the air. The celebrations. A successful Test Championship final. (Nickolaus) The home of cricket, the World Test Championship final and South Africa versus Australia. Another opportunity to exorcise the choking curse as a Proteas fan. I'm going to leave nothing to chance. I'm even wearing my lucky socks! (Nickolaus) Supporting the Proteas has become an exercise in generational trauma. From sheer bad luck, rain and the dreaded Duckworth-Lewis scoring system to batting capitulations and demolitions of our bowling. The Proteas have always found a way to snatch defeat from the jaws of victory. (Voxie Female 1) Respect on both sides, but SA is going to bring the cup home, I’m afraid. (Nickolaus) Lord’s, generally regarded as cricket’s spiritual home, would be the stage for yet another shot at glory. (Archive Upsound) What an uptake. (Nickolaus) Altogether, the Proteas have failed 13 times in global tournaments over 33 years. It’s a record cricket correspondent, Daniel Gallan says is impossible to ignore every time they play. (Daniel Gallan) So many heartaches - 92 in the rain, Allan Donald dropped bat in 99, the poor maths in 2003, New Zealand chokes losing to the Netherlands, India last year in the T20 final. I guess we South African cricket fans who have suffered for so long feel like we're due one maybe. (Nickolaus) How does this Proteas team stack up against the others that couldn’t get across the line? (Daniel Gallan) I think that they're more than the sum of their parts. I think there's a sense of unity. I think there's a collective. And I think that, unlike previous iterations… I maybe have strong memories of past chokes. They are free from this narrative. At least, that's the line that they're trying to cultivate. And I do think there's a sincerity in that. (Nickolaus) London is a long way from Cape Town, Durban and Johannesburg. But that didn’t stop these fans from making their way here. (Voxie Male 1) We’re South Africans, we love sports. It's in our DNA. (Voxie Female 2) They're an awesome team. And we've got to get behind our boys. And they're only going to win if we come and support them and cheer them on. (Voxie Male 2) We win, we win. If we lose, we take it on the chin. (Voxie Male 3) Yes, there’s been heartache. Yes, there’s been very, very tough times. But again, you wake up, dust yourself off and you go again. (Voxie Male 4) Hopefully, you can split the choke out consistently over five days. (Voxie Male 5) Temba Bavuma! Wonderful! (Nickolaus) Could it be the Test World Championship - a tournament including the top nine teams in the game’s longest format - that would finally deliver victory? As a diehard Proteas fan myself, I hoped so. (Nickolaus) The limitless optimism of Proteas fans didn’t do much to better the odds of them finally winning a trophy. William Kedjanyi is a bookie specialising in cricket betting. (Nickolaus) I'm loath to use the C-word, but we haven't had the best record when it comes to knockout games. How do you think that's going to affect the odds? (William Kedanyi) Some people have labelled the Proteas a bottling premium, even in betting circles, waiting for them to choke so it improves their position. But I think this time, people might just be overrating that factor a little bit. You have to treat each game as it is. There are factors that will push prices and bring them in. (Nickolaus) So, if I'm a betting man, what are the odds for the Proteas against Australia? (William Kedanyi) They are 25%, or 3 to 1. Now look, that will seem low. It will seem pessimistic. But it's not really against the Proteas. It's Australia. The guys going in there, they'll know exactly what they're doing. And it's not to say South Africa won't, but you look at it, it's a very menacing line-up. (Nickolaus) In other words: don’t bet on the Proteas unless you’re comfortable losing your money. Something I’m certainly not. (Nickolaus) While they might have been against us, I still felt confident our team would beat the odds. Finally turning the tide on a losing habit that began back at the 1992 World Cup in Australia. After cruising to victory in a match against England, the weather intervened, leaving us needing 22 runs off just one ball. (David Richardson) Back in those days, you had a profession and played cricket. (Nickolaus) You were a lawyer, weren’t you? (David Richardson) Yes, I was. (Nickolaus) Former Proteas wicket-keeper, David Richardson was at the crease at the time. (David Richardson) It's something that I look back on and think, “Gee! That was an opportunity that was missed.” (Nickolaus) Sometimes, it feels as though the Proteas are cursed. (David Richardson) Well, maybe there is a curse. Who knows? But I still think that in their heart and soul, in the moment they are competing and it’s not a case of them just wilting under pressure. I think it's something that will either go your way or not. And you do need a bit of luck. On many occasions, even to the best to actually get over the line. (Archive Upsound) South Africa against Australia. The sun is shining on Lord’s Cricket Ground. It is set up perfectly. (Nickolaus) Armed with my accreditation, I joined hundreds of media from around the world covering the match. (Archive Upsound) It is a batting day. (Nickolaus) But compared to the stiffness of the media centre, the gees of the stands was hard to resist. (Nickolaus) Duty calls. (Nickolaus) Let’s go! (Archive Upsound) Two top sides and a great format. Test match cricket is back! (Nickolaus) Lord’s is hallowed ground for any cricket fan. And for the week of the Test Championship, it took on a distinctly South African flavour. (Nickolaus Subtitles) A little taste of home, hey? (Vendor Subtitles) The boerewors is sold out. They are… (Nickolaus Subtitles) Sold out of Boerewors! Sold out of Boerewors! (Nickolaus) Prior to the tournament, questions had been raised about whether we deserved to be in the final at all, not having played against all the sport’s top teams. We went into the game against a powerful Australian side as solid underdogs. (Nickolaus) As Temba Bavuma led us into battle, I took my place in the stands. (Nickolaus) After the Aussies were put in to bat, our bowling attack didn’t disappoint. (Archive Upsound) And there it is. What a moment for Kagiso Rabada. (Nickolaus) Restricting Australia to 212 in their first innings after an aggressive KG Rabada took 5 wickets. (Archive Upsound) So, wickets continue to tumble after lunch. It’s 137 for 8. (Nickolaus) Then, as had been the case so often before, optimism gave way to frustration as the Aussie bowlers had us all out for 138… 74 runs behind! The ghosts of past failures came back to haunt me. (Archive Upsound) Bowled-out South Africa out for 138. Which gives them a very healthy lead of 74. (Nickolaus) Our cricket team is the opposite of fairytale character Peter Pan, which doesn't exist unless you believe in it. The Proteas, on the other hand, fail to exist the moment you believe in them. Why? (Nickolaus) Why had the Proteas managed to flop every single time it mattered since 1992? (Nickolaus) Sports psychologist Kitrina Douglas had some interesting thoughts. (Kitrina Douglas) I'm curious to see how all the other cricket teams’ story, their experiences, their losses… And I'd be interested to look at the games that you are winning and what's happening there and how that is storied by the media, by the press, by the fans. Is that given a negative slant? (Nickolaus) Hang on, Professor. You’re saying that we, the fans, are the problem? (Kitrina Douglas) Yes, I am actually. And I think psychology more recently has expanded to realise that it's not just about what happens inside here. It's about what happens in your immediate subculture, in the culture and society what cricket means for them. Because the dominant narrative is it's all about winning, it's all about being the best. And that's what we want. And anything short of that is failure. So, I think the first thing is to support the players, whatever, and not put your expectations on them. (Crowd) Oh, Temba Bavuma! Oh, Temba Bavuma! (Nickolaus) Doing my best to heed the advice, I headed back to the stands. What followed was a pulsating four days of test cricket, not all of it easy to watch. (Archive Upsound) Frustration again. Just dabbed away up the hill. (Nickolaus) Our bowlers again pulled off a minor miracle in restricting Australia to 207 in their second innings, leaving a small window to victory - 282 needed for an improbable win. (Nickolaus) Then Bavuma, after a reasonable score in the first innings, look set for an early departure after apparently pulling a leg muscle. (Nickolaus) And, after being out for a duck in his first knock, opening batsman Aiden Markram was hardly inspiring confidence in the traveling fans. (Nickolaus) But our captain played through the pain, scoring runs and providing support to Makram who stuck it to his critics by scoring a brilliant century. (Archive Upsound) And if South Africa go on to win this game, it will be his most important. (Archive Upsound) Fantastic performance here by Aiden Markram. (Archive Upsound) Verreyne does the honours. And South Africa make history. (Nickolaus) After a nail-biting few sessions of cricket, the Proteas finally broke the curse, beating Australia by five wickets and becoming the 2025 World Test Championship winners. (Archive Upsound) South Africa! (Nickolaus) Choke no more! (Daniel Gallan) I truly think this could be the greatest moment in South African cricket history. (Nickolaus) For the man that led the way to breaking the curse with a disciplined 136 in the second innings, it was a moment to savour. (Aiden Markram) Just to see the smiles on faces and the happy vibes from everyone supporting us has been really cool. A lot of this victory goes towards them. Those that have been there through thick and thin for us. And it's just as special for them as it is for us. (Nickolaus) The Proteas can finally call themselves champions. Champions against Australia in the world test championship final at Lord’s.

metadata.Summary: For decades, the Proteas have found heartbreak in the most imaginative ways possible, from farcical rain rules in 1992 to boundary drama in 2023. Now, with the World Test Championship final against Australia set at the iconic Lord’s Cricket Ground, can the national team finally exorcise the ghosts of cricketing trauma past? Told through the eyes of a long-suffering Proteas fan, this piece is part comedy, part catharsis — a generational therapy session disguised as a cricket feature. It’s a story about hope, heartbreak, and the strange, stubborn love of South African fans who keep coming back for more.
metadata.Further information: Key Themes: The Curse of the Proteas: Revisiting South Africa’s most painful cricketing moments: 1992: 22 needed off 1 ball vs. England 1996: Brian Lara’s masterclass knocks us out 1999: Allan Donald drops his bat, World Cup dream dies 2003: Shaun Pollock misreads Duckworth-Lewis 2007: Batting collapse against Australia 2011: Demolished by the Pakistanis 2015: Rain, heartbreak, and Elliott’s six 2023: David Miller's boundary catch — out or over? The Psychology of Choking: Can national trauma be inherited? Is performance pressure a self-fulfilling prophecy? What makes teams crumble — and what might finally help us break through? Fans on the Edge: For South Africans who’ve travelled the world to watch the Proteas, this isn’t just another match. It’s a spiritual reckoning. Hope, Humor, and Holding On: From bookies giving odds on a classic South African collapse, to fan parks full of cheering (and weeping) expats — this is a love story, set to leather and willow. Visual Approach: Bookends at Lord’s: Opening shot: the hallowed Long Room at Lord’s on Day 1 — Nickolaus in full fan regalia. Closing shot: same spot on Day 5 — outcome unknown, but the heart remains. Fan Parks, Living Rooms & Labs: Footage of Sipho Van Der Merwe waving a flag in the crowd and FaceTiming his family back home Animated reenactments of cricket heartbreaks (think: comic-style renderings of Donald’s runout, Lara’s boundary blitz) A quirky interview with Thomas Winalot, taking absurd bets on new ways South Africa might lose Interview scenes with Prof. Winter, surrounded by data, graphs, and slow-mo collapses Nostalgic cricket archive visuals: broken stumps, stunned faces, flying bails Voice, Tone, and Music: Hopeful yet haunted. A mix of emotional scoring and cheeky cricketing commentary Daniel Gallan providing the voice of weary, informed optimism Ntini as the heartbeat of belief: “This is the one.” Scene Breakdown: Scene 1: Day One – The Wait Begins Location: Lord’s Cricket Ground, London Nickolaus Bauer (PTC): “They say hope is a dangerous thing. For Proteas fans, it’s also hereditary. But here we are again — finals day, full of belief, with just a little PTSD.” VO: "Thirty years. Five formats. One long heartbreak. The Proteas have made a habit of turning opportunity into agony." Scene 2: A Fan’s Tale Location: Tube ride to Lord’s, then the stands Sipho Van Der Merwe: “I’ve mortgaged my sanity to this team. But I wouldn’t miss this for the world. This could be the day we finally heal.” Scene 3: Trauma in HD Location: Studio reenactments & archive clips VO: “1992. Rain falls, hopes drown. 1999. One bat drop, one heartbreak. 2023. A toe on the rope, a nation weeps.” Pollock (reflecting): “We were so close. But sometimes, the weight of history... you feel it.” Scene 4: The Choke Explained Location: Academic lab Prof. Stacy Winter: “Choking isn’t about skill. It’s about what happens when self-doubt hijacks performance. South Africa? They've built an identity around almost.” Scene 5: The Bookmaker’s Bet Location: London betting shop Thomas Winalot: “Odds of SA collapsing from a winning position? We’ve got a name for that: the Proteas Special.” (laughs) Scene 6: The Final Hour Location: Lord’s, Day 5 VO: "Whether it ends in triumph or tears, this is the price of believing. Because to be a Proteas fan is to love without condition." Scene 7: Ending – After the Final Ball Location: Long Room at Lord’s, sunset Nickolaus Bauer (PTC): “We laughed. We cried. We hoped. And no matter the result, we’ll be back next time. Because this team? This pain? It’s family.” Outcome Possibilities: If Proteas Win: "We exorcised the demon." Emotional montages, fans crying, Ntini dancing in the stands, Daniel Gallan speechless. If Proteas Lose: "What did you expect?" Sipho eating a wors roll in silence, a child with a broken vuvuzela, bookie paying out smug bets — and Nickolaus quietly hopeful for 2029
